input: It is also worth pausing to consider the Chilton-Colburn analogy in a little more depth, because it provides an extremely useful bridge between the transfer processes that have been discussed so far. In essence, the Chilton-Colburn analogy tells us that the mass-transfer factor $j_D$ is equal to half of the friction factor $f$, and this simple relationship can be very powerful in practice. To illustrate this, we can work through a short numerical check using some values that are already in hand. Suppose, for example, that we are dealing with a Reynolds number of 20000 and a measured friction factor $f$ of 0.0064; applying the analogy then gives us $j_D$ = 0.0032, which is simply half of the friction factor, and the mass-transfer coefficient can then be obtained from that figure by following the route that was set out earlier in the chapter. It is important to note, however, that this equality is by no means universal, and there are situations in which it begins to break down. In particular, where form drag makes a contribution to the friction factor, the friction factor effectively includes an element that has no real counterpart on the mass-transfer side, and under those circumstances $j_D$ will tend to fall below $f$ / 2. Similarly, where the transfer rate becomes high enough to alter the boundary layer itself, the equality can again be expected to fail. So the check that has just been worked, with $f$ = 0.0064 and $j_D$ = 0.0032 at a Reynolds number of 20000, really only confirms the arithmetic of the analogy on that one pair of values, and it should not be taken as extending the analogy into cases involving form drag or high transfer rates.
target: The Chilton-Colburn analogy sets the mass-transfer factor $j_D$ equal to half the friction factor $f$, and the equality is the working form in which the analogy is used for design. A short check shows the arithmetic on values already in hand. At a Reynolds number of 20000, a measured friction factor $f$ of 0.0064 gives $j_D$ = 0.0032, half the friction factor, and a design calculation takes the mass-transfer coefficient from that figure by the route set out earlier in the chapter. The three transfer processes fall under one analogy because each is carried across the same boundary layer: momentum crosses it by friction, and mass crosses it by diffusion and convection together, so a measurement of the one process can be made to speak for the other wherever the layer behaves alike for both. The equality is not a law, and its range is the range of the conditions that produced it. The analogy rests on the boundary layer behaving the same way for momentum and for mass, and it fails where that behaviour separates. Where form drag contributes to the friction factor, $f$ carries a part that has no counterpart in mass transfer, and $j_D$ falls below $f$ / 2. Where the transfer rate is high enough to change the boundary layer itself, the equality again fails, in the same direction: the friction factor describes the flow that was measured, and the mass transfer is no longer the transfer of that flow. The check above therefore has a narrow use. It verifies the arithmetic of the analogy on one pair of values ($f$ = 0.0064, $j_D$ = 0.0032 at a Reynolds number of 20000); it does not extend the analogy to any case where form drag or a high transfer rate is in play, and a calculation that meets either condition needs its mass-transfer factor from measurement or from a correlation built for that case.
